Lesson 2.1: Hazard Detection and Observation Skills
Lesson 4.1: Night and Subdued Light Driving
q: A field training officer tells a recruit why patrol driving is harder than everyday driving. Which pair of demands does she name?
Driving in emergency mode while talking with dispatch
Steering with a tactical harness on and a radio in hand
Filling out inspection forms while checking fluid levels
Backing through courses while watching the rear camera

Patrol driving adds demands that ordinary driving does not: emergency-mode driving, talking with dispatch and tracking what other drivers do; the course teaches the vehicle's limits and the officer's own limits.
Besides vehicle limits, which two things does the course say officers should understand about themselves as drivers?
How their eyesight changes with age and how often they need new lenses
How stress affects their driving and how the public sees them
How weather affects braking and how ABS changes their stopping distance
How their agency writes its policy and how the courts later review it
Officers need to know how physical and mental stress affect their driving and how the public sees them as drivers.
A new officer asks what a full vehicle inspection covers. Which answer is complete?
Fluids, hoses, wiring, belts and tires, with nothing else added
Interior, exterior, the radio and the emergency lights, nothing more
Tires, rims, glass, mirrors and the undercarriage, and nothing more
Fluids, hoses, wiring, belts, tires, interior and exterior
A vehicle inspection covers fluid levels, hoses, electrical wiring, belts and tires, plus the interior and the exterior.
Your agency hands you a checklist to complete every time you take a fleet car. What two jobs does it do?
Lists the six fluids and each manufacturer's recommended level
Records your mileage and keeps a log of your fuel purchases
Tracks your pursuits and records every unit that was involved
Reminds you what to check and lets you report failing gear
Most agencies require officers to fill out an inspection form whenever they use an agency vehicle; it reminds them what to check and lets them report equipment that is failing.
Your agency expects officers to change a burned-out bulb themselves, while another agency wants the shop notified. Which part of the inspection form serves both?
The mileage line
The signature block
The fuel log
The comments section

Agencies handle failing equipment differently: some want a written report, some expect officers to fix small things themselves (change a tire or bulb, add fluids), and some want a certain repair shop notified; the form's comments section serves all of these.
Why does the chapter say problems must be found before a patrol car goes on the road?
Its emergency lights drain the fuel tank faster than normal driving
Its warranty requires a written inspection at the start of each day
Its tires are kept inflated below the level listed on the doorjamb
It is driven in far harsher conditions than a personal car
A patrol vehicle is driven in far harsher conditions than a personal car, so problems must be found and repaired before it goes on the road.
An officer skips her pre-shift check, and a cracked hose she would have caught bursts during a call. What does the chapter warn this can create?
A special relationship with the next driver who uses the car
A negligence review of the officer under the Fourth Amendment
A pursuit-reporting duty that falls under the agency's policy
Liability, besides a policy violation and a missed hazard

Inspect the vehicle before and after every use; skipping or rushing the inspection can miss safety hazards, break agency policy and create liability when a problem an inspection would have caught causes harm.
Walking around the car, you find a fresh dent in the rear door. What does a dent suggest compared with a scratch?
A tire problem caused by improper balance or alignment
A clearer sign of contact, maybe with another vehicle
A broken cover that may count as a traffic violation
Probable intentional damage done to the paint by someone

The exterior check is a quick look at the body and undercarriage: scratched paint can mean contact with an object or deliberate damage, and dents are a clearer sign of contact, possibly with another vehicle.
A taillight cover on your patrol car is cracked away. What two problems can this cause?
A failed siren and no way to run the car in emergency mode
A slow fluid leak and a steady drop in the battery's charge
A hazard to other drivers and a possible traffic violation
Blocked vision for you and a real chance of cutting yourself
A missing or broken light cover can put other motorists at risk and can itself be a traffic violation.
During inspection, the light bar flickers and dies. Why does the chapter treat this as serious?
It shows the tires can no longer shed water at all
It means the coolant reservoir has dropped too low
It is usually the first sign of a grass fire below
It could keep you from operating in emergency mode
A damaged or malfunctioning siren, light bar or other emergency light could keep the vehicle from running in emergency mode.
Which exterior problem does the chapter say could both injure you and block your view?
Scratched paint on the body
Missing or broken light covers
Broken or cracked glass
A dirty or smeared windshield
Broken or cracked glass can injure the driver and block vision; cracked or broken mirrors and a dirty windshield also hurt the ability to see and observe.
A broken branch is wedged under your car's frame. Why remove it before driving?
It changes the tire PSI on that side
It may be a harmful device that requires backing away
It can cause serious damage if it hits a moving part
It can blind other drivers at night
Tree limbs and road debris caught under the vehicle can cause serious damage if they hit a moving part.
During your walk-around you see a wrapped object taped under the gas tank that is clearly not road debris. What is your next step?
Photograph it where it is and then drive to the station
Start the engine to see whether it falls off on its own
Back away and contact the personnel your agency designates
Remove it carefully with gloves and secure it in the trunk
Something under the vehicle that is not natural debris, such as a possible explosive, means back away and contact the personnel your agency's policy names.
Where does the chapter tell you to look for fluid leaks during the exterior check?
On the ground beneath the vehicle
Inside the coolant reservoir's cap
Under the back seat behind the cage
Along the belts and the radiator hoses
Look for fluid leaks on the ground beneath the vehicle.
The inside edge of your front tire is worn smooth while the rest has tread. Which causes does the chapter list for uneven wear?
Balance, alignment, over inflation or under inflation
Hydroplaning, wet brakes, standing water or deep puddles
Embedded objects, cuts, sidewall bulges or bead damage
Heavy braking, wheel spin, incipient spin or hard starts
Uneven tire wear can come from poor balance or alignment, over inflation or under inflation, and can make the vehicle hard to handle.
You want to check whether your tires are properly inflated. Where does the chapter say the recommended PSI is listed?
On the dashboard
On the tire sidewall
In the inspection form
On the doorjamb
Tire inflation is measured in PSI (pounds per square inch); tires should be at or above the manufacturer's recommended PSI, which is listed on the doorjamb.
The wear bars on your tire are now flush with the tread. What can the tire no longer do?
Hold the manufacturer's recommended PSI
Keep the bead seated on the rim
Move water and other fluids away
Absorb the caster effect in turns
Once the wear bars sit flush with the tread, the tire can no longer channel water and other fluids away.
A screw is lodged in the tread of your patrol car's tire. What does the chapter tell you to do?
Leave it in place and keep driving until the end of the shift
Leave it in and let maintenance or the dealer remove it
Pull it out and refill the tire to the doorjamb's listed PSI
Pull it out yourself only if the tire is not losing any air
Do not pull out an object stuck in a tire; it can deflate the tire or cause a blowout, so leave removal to the dealer or maintenance staff, who should also check any sidewall bulges.
When checking the rims, which damage does the chapter name?
Dry rot, holes, bulges or slow leaks
Fraying, cuts, deep cracks or gouges
Dents, cracks or damage to the bead
Fraying, corrosion or bare, exposed wire
Cuts in a tire can lead to a blowout and need attention; also check the rims for dents, cracks or damage to the bead.
While driving, the car pulls hard to the left and the steering wheel shakes. Which tire most likely failed?
The right front tire
The right rear tire
The left rear tire
The left front tire
A failed front tire can cost traction, make steering hard, shake the steering wheel and pull the vehicle toward the failed tire.
How does the chapter describe the pull from a failed rear tire?
It shakes the steering wheel violently in your hands
It pulls the car steadily toward the side of the failed tire
It makes the car straighten itself out of every turn
It may pull the car in an unpredictable direction
A failed rear tire can also cost traction and pull the vehicle in an unpredictable direction.
The exterior looks perfect, so a recruit wants to skip the hood. What does the chapter say?
Check under the hood only once a week
Never drive without checking under the hood
Let the dealer check under the hood monthly
Check under the hood only if a gauge looks wrong
Never drive without checking under the hood; every fluid should be at the manufacturer's recommended level.
How often should hoses, wires and belts be inspected?
Once a week at the start of a shift
Only after a pursuit or emergency response
Whenever the coolant reservoir is low
Every day before the vehicle is driven
Hoses, wires and belts should be checked every day before the vehicle is driven.
Under the hood, you are checking a belt. Which set of problems are you looking for?
Fraying, corrosion and missing insulation
Fraying, cuts, cracks and gouges
Dry rot, cracks, holes, bulges and leaks
Dents, cracks and damage to the bead
Check belts for fraying, cuts, cracks and gouges.
You squeeze a radiator hose to inspect it. Which set of problems belongs to hoses?
Dry rot, cracks, holes, bulges and leaks
Uneven wear, cuts and bulges on the sidewall
Fraying, cuts, cracks and gouges
Fraying, corrosion and exposed wire
Check hoses for dry rot, cracks, holes, bulges and leaks.
Checking the wiring, which problems does the chapter tell you to look for?
Loose terminal connections, a low water level and a damaged case
Dry rot, holes, bulges and slow leaks at each of the connections
Fraying, corrosion, cracked or missing insulation and exposure
Fraying, cuts, cracks and deep gouges along the whole length
Check wires for fraying, corrosion, cracked or missing insulation and exposed wire.
Why does the chapter single out the battery in a patrol car?
Radios and emergency gear put a heavy strain on it
Hot Florida weather makes it the most common part to fail
Its water level is what sets the coolant reservoir's level
Long pursuits cause it to fade the same way the brakes do
Radios and emergency equipment put a heavy load on the battery, so check its terminal connections, water level where it has one and the outside of the case for damage.
Your coffee cup and flashlight sit loose on the passenger seat. Why does the chapter say to secure them?
They interfere with the radio's ability to send and receive
They can block the passenger airbag from deploying in a crash
They travel at the car's speed and become hazards in a sudden stop
They throw the vehicle's weight distribution badly off balance
Loose items such as briefcases, flashlights and coffee cups move at the vehicle's speed and become dangerous in a sudden stop, so stow and secure all equipment.
What should you check the seats for during the interior inspection?
Tears or other damage
Fraying and binding belts
Dents and deep scratches
Dry rot and small cracks
Check the seats for tears or other damage.
You just dropped an arrestee at the jail. What must you check before taking another call?
The cargo area for long items stored front to back
The tire wear bars on the rear tires
The battery's terminal connections
Under the back seat for weapons or contraband
At the start and end of every shift, and after each prisoner transport, search under the back seat for weapons or contraband left behind by a suspect.
Testing a seat belt, which problems do you look for?
Corrosion, exposed wire and cracked or missing insulation
Tears in the fabric and other damage to the seat itself
Cracks in the webbing and bulges in the buckle's housing
Fraying, binding and a buckle that will not latch
Look for frayed or binding seat belts and confirm that each buckle latches.
Which lights does the chapter tell you to test during the interior check?
Interior lights, dashboard lights and the rear backup camera
Headlights, interior lights, turn signals and hazard flashers
The light bar, the spotlight, the siren and the turn signals
Headlights, brake lights, fog lights and the roof light bar
Test the headlights, interior lights, turn signals and hazard flashers, and check that the rearview mirror is firmly attached and not cracked or broken.
Before going in service, what does the chapter say to confirm about the radio?
That the volume is high enough to hear over the siren
That it is set to the primary dispatch channel
That its antenna is clear of tree limbs
That you can both send and receive transmissions
Test the radio so you know you can send and receive, and make sure the windows and door locks work.
You turn the key and the fuel needle does not move. What does the chapter say about the gauges?
Only the temperature gauge needs to respond when the car starts
The fuel and battery gauges should move when the car is turned on
Gauge problems belong on the separate cargo-area checklist
The fuel gauge should read full before the start of every shift
Look over the gauges for damage and confirm they respond; the fuel and battery needles should move once the ignition is on.
Which items make up the emergency equipment the chapter tells you to test?
Horn, siren and light bar
Horn, headlights and backup camera
Light bar, hazard flashers and turn signals
Siren, spotlight and radio
Test the emergency equipment: horn, siren and light bar.
After the initial inspection you start the engine. What should you watch for?
Whether the ABS brake pedal pulses each time you press it
Whether the tires start to spin as soon as you press the gas
Unusual sounds, smells or other signs that need a closer look
Whether the caster effect straightens the wheel on its own
After the first inspection, start the engine, check the windows and doors again, and pay attention to strange sounds or smells that call for a closer look.
The engine is running and you want to check for leaks. Where do you stand?
Inside the car, watching the gauges on the dashboard
Behind the rear bumper, right beside the exhaust pipe
In front of the bumper, for the clearest view below
At the side of the vehicle, never in front of it
With the engine running, look under the vehicle for leaks that only show when it is running, standing at the side of the vehicle, never in front of it; then you can shut the engine off.
Opening the trunk, which items does the chapter say should be there?
A jack, a first-aid kit, a long gun and a tow strap
A spare battery, washer fluid, oil and coolant
A spare tire, jack, tire tool and agency duty gear
A spare tire, flares, a fire extinguisher and cones
The trunk, cargo area or bed should carry a spare, a jack, a tire tool and the duty gear your agency usually issues.
Gear slides around loose in your cargo area. What two problems does the chapter warn about?
It can block the rear camera and set off the car alarm
It can puncture both the gas tank and the spare tire
It can damage the vehicle or change how it handles
It can strain the battery and interfere with the radio
Secure everything in the cargo area, because shifting gear can damage the vehicle or change how it handles.
You load a shotgun and a long pry bar into the trunk. How should they be stored, and why?
Side to side, so a rear-end crash cannot drive them forward
On the back seat instead, so the trunk weight stays even
Front to back, so they lie flat and do not shift during turns
Upright against the seat back, so they are quick to reach
Store long items such as long guns and long-handled tools side to side across the cargo area, not front to back, so a rear-end crash cannot push them into the passenger compartment or the gas tank.
An instructor admits you cannot predict every driver's actions. What does the chapter say observation skills do instead?
Replace the need for scanning
Remove the risk at intersections
Prepare you to react
Let you avoid every hazard
You cannot predict every driver or hazard, but better observation and driving skills prepare you to react.
Which two tips open NHTSA's Countermeasures That Work list?
Use the three-second rule and scan thoroughly before turning
Wear your seat belt every time and never rely only on airbags
Learn to spot hazardous situations and assume others will err
Drive at or below the speed limit and eat smaller meals often
NHTSA's guide Countermeasures That Work gives crash-prevention tips: learn to recognize hazardous driving situations and assume other drivers will make mistakes.
Which NHTSA tip tells you to change how you drive so you can move safely if a hazard appears?
Scan thoroughly before changing speed or direction
Scan far enough ahead to react safely
Scan often to the side and rear
Adjust speed, position, direction and attention
Adjust your speed, position, direction and attention so you can move safely if a hazard appears.
You keep reacting late to traffic backups. Which NHTSA tip addresses this?
Assume other drivers will make errors
Scan far enough ahead to react safely
Scan thoroughly before changing direction
Scan often to the side and rear
Scan far enough ahead to react safely to what is coming.
A car keeps appearing in your blind spot without warning. Which NHTSA tip would help?
Adjust your speed and lane position
Scan far enough ahead to react
Learn to recognize hazardous situations
Scan frequently to the side and rear
Scan often to the side and rear for vehicles that are passing or approaching.
Before you change lanes or brake for a turn, which NHTSA tip applies?
Scan frequently, but only to the rear of the vehicle
Scan far enough ahead to react safely to what comes
Assume that other drivers on the road will make errors
Scan thoroughly before changing speed or direction
Scan carefully before you change speed or direction.
What does the chapter say you should use to detect and confirm a possible hazard or vehicle problem?
Your dash camera
Your partner's report
Your inspection form
Your senses
Use your senses to detect and confirm a hazard or vehicle problem and be ready to react to other drivers and road hazards.
Mid-shift, you notice smoke from under your hood. What does the chapter tell you to do?
Pull off to a safe location and notify dispatch
Keep driving and note it on the inspection form
Drive to the nearest fire station with lights on
Stop in the lane and open the hood at once
If you find a safety hazard with the vehicle, pull off the road to a safe place and notify dispatch (the public safety telecommunicator), following agency policy.
About how much of the information a driver takes in comes from vision?
About 75 to 80 percent
About 90 to 95 percent
About 50 to 55 percent
About 60 to 65 percent
Vision provides roughly 90 to 95 percent of the information a driver takes in and helps detect and avoid hazards.
A recruit's eye exam shows he reads distant signs blurry. Which component of vision is affected?
Depth perception
Peripheral vision
Color vision
Acuity
Acuity is how sharp your vision is.
A driver keeps misjudging how far away the car ahead is. Which component of vision is involved?
Depth perception
Night vision
Acuity
Peripheral vision
Depth perception is judging distance and space to tell how far away an object is.
Sitting in a stopped patrol car with good peripheral vision, about how wide a view can you take in?
About 90 degrees
About 270 degrees
About 180 degrees
About 120 degrees
Peripheral vision lets you see up, down and off to each side; with good peripheral vision, a seated driver in a stopped car takes in about 180 degrees.
Which pair of vision components does the chapter define as telling colors apart and seeing clearly in the dark?
Depth perception and acuity
Peripheral vision and night vision
Color vision and night vision
Acuity and peripheral vision
Color vision is telling colors apart, and night vision is seeing clearly in the dark.
Which factors does the chapter say affect vision?
Environment, physical condition, alertness and aging
Shift length, meal size, radio volume and cabin heat
Tire wear, window tint, road surface and lane width
Seat position, mirror angle, hand position and grip
Environmental and physical conditions, alertness and aging all affect vision; have your eyes checked regularly and correct problems with lenses before driving.
Besides eyesight itself, which two outside factors does the chapter say change how much you can see?
Fatigue and stress
Vehicle speed and glare
Engine noise and road surface
Wind and rain
How fast you are going, sun glare and glare from other lights also change how much you can see.
Why does the chapter mention heavily tinted windows?
Tint hides the car's inspection sticker from your view
Approaching such a car is a safety hazard for officers
Tint is the leading single cause of night-time crashes
Tint is what makes the six-second rule necessary
Tinted glass reduces visibility, and approaching a car whose windows are heavily tinted puts an officer at risk.
A pedestrian steps off the curb mid-block in front of you. What does the chapter say about such hazards?
They are less dangerous than animals at dusk
They are the single greatest threat to safe driving
They can require immediate action from the driver
They call for the six-second following rule
Pedestrians who cross at unexpected places can demand an immediate reaction.
Which road users does the chapter say share the lanes and sometimes fall?
Bicyclists and motorcyclists
Joggers and dog walkers
School buses and delivery vans
Pedestrians and street vendors
Bicyclists and motorcyclists share the lanes and sometimes fall, and skateboarders and roller skaters can fall too.
A cat darts across the road in front of your patrol car. What does the chapter warn about swerving or stopping hard?
It is what your agency's policy requires you to do
It may cause worse damage than hitting the animal
It is always safe at or below the posted speed limit
It is always safe as long as you use shuffle steering
Hitting a large animal is clearly dangerous, but suddenly stopping or swerving for a small animal can cause worse damage than hitting it.
Driving a rural road at dusk, which animals does the chapter say add risk then?
Deer, black bears and alligators
Opossums, raccoons and armadillos
Stray dogs, feral cats and horses
Squirrels, rabbits and wild turkeys
Animals most active at dusk or at night, such as opossums, raccoons and armadillos, add risk.
Which vehicle-related dangers does the chapter list among road hazards?
Cars carrying loose cargo and cars running on badly worn tires
Cars with heavily tinted windows and cars with no inspection sticker
Cars parked so they block the road and cars that pull out suddenly
Cars driving at or below the posted speed limit in the right lane
Cars parked so they block the road, and cars that dart into traffic or block your view, are road hazards.
Which roadway conditions does the chapter name as safety threats?
Streetlights, road signs, mailboxes and guardrails
Speed bumps, rumble strips and faded painted lines
Obstructions, surface damage, debris and fluid
Toll booths, drawbridges and long highway tunnels
Roadway obstructions, surface flaws or damage, debris and fluid on the road are also threats.
Hearing helps you find sounds that may mean what?
A failed tire, a weak battery or brakes that got wet
A vehicle problem, a suspicious incident or a crime
An oncoming car, a hidden curve or a hill up ahead
A change in the road surface, the weather or the traffic
Hearing helps you find sounds that may mean a vehicle problem, a suspicious incident or a crime.
You hear breaking glass but can't tell where it came from because of tall buildings around you. What does the chapter suggest?
Drive faster so you can get closer to the sound
Scan visually to find the source and direction
Close all your windows to cut down on the echo
Turn off the engine and listen for it once more
Open or closed windows and nearby buildings can make a sound hard to locate; when unsure, scan visually to find where it is coming from.
Why does the chapter recommend patrolling with the driver's window down?
It keeps the cabin cool so that you stay awake and alert
You can hear and see trouble and hear other responding units
It lowers the glare you get from oncoming headlights at night
It keeps the inside of the windshield from fogging up at night

Driving with the driver's window down helps you hear and see people who need help, crimes in progress and suspicious activity, and warns you of fire trucks, rescue units and other police heading to the same scene.
You notice an unusual smell while driving. What is the first thing to decide?
Whether it comes from your car or from outside
Whether it matches the smell of gasoline or propane
Whether you can finish your current call first
Whether all of the windows should be rolled up
When you smell an unusual odor, decide whether it comes from the patrol car or from outside, and look for smoke or another source.
You smell an odor you can't identify. It isn't smoke, gasoline or propane. What do you do?
Get out, get clear and call more resources
Note it now and check on it after the shift ends
Drive on to the call with all the windows closed
Search the whole car for the source by yourself
If the odor is not as easy to identify as smoke, gasoline or propane, get out of the vehicle and call more resources to investigate; get clear of the possible hazard first.
You park over a grassy shoulder for an hour with the engine idling. What can happen, and what is the first sign?
A dead battery from the light bar, warned by dim and flickering gauges
A grass fire from the catalytic converter, warned by a bitter smell
A tire blowout from the hot pavement, warned by a bulge on the sidewall
An overheated engine from low coolant, warned by steam from the hood
A car left idling over grass for a long time can set the grass on fire, usually from the heat of the catalytic converter; a bitter smoky smell is normally the first warning.
Your steering wheel pulls steadily to the right. What does touch tell you this may be?
A low brake fluid level
An alignment problem
A failed rear tire
A steering or tire problem
Touch gives feedback on handling: an excessively vibrating steering wheel can mean a steering or tire problem, and a wheel that pulls one way can mean an alignment problem.
Something feels off with the car while driving. What three checks does the chapter list?
Test the brakes, check the steering, look for smoke or fire
Check the engine oil, the coolant and the washer fluid levels
Check the tire PSI, the tread wear bars and the rims for dents
Test the horn, the siren and the light bar one after another
If you sense something unusual while driving, check whether it is a safety concern: press the brake to confirm it works, check the steering and look for smoke or an engine fire.
Which speed habit does the chapter say helps you observe and respond to your surroundings?
Driving under the limit only at night
Driving at or below the posted limit
Driving five over to keep up with traffic
Matching the speed of the car ahead
Keeping to the speed limit or a little under it gives you time to notice and react to what is around you.
A night-shift deputy eats one huge meal before work and sleeps only four hours. What does the chapter recommend instead?
One large meal after the shift and plenty of caffeine during it
Skipping meals entirely and napping in the patrol car on breaks
A large breakfast before bed and an early bedtime on days off
Smaller, more frequent meals and enough sleep before a shift
Adjust meals and habits to stay alert: eat smaller meals more often through the day, and sleep and rest well before a shift so you do not drive drowsy.
A recruit takes an over-the-counter cold pill before driving. What does the chapter warn medicines like this can do?
Raise the risk of hydroplaning in rain
Speed up the caster effect in turns
Affect observation and reaction time
Strain the patrol vehicle's battery
Prescription drugs, over-the-counter medicine and bad driving habits can slow observation and reaction time and lead to inattention, lost control and crashes.
Which group does the chapter list as road surface hazards?
Oncoming headlights, streetlights, smoke and drifting patches of fog
Potholes, sinkholes, curbs and railroad tracks met without warning
Pedestrians, bicyclists, skateboarders and roller skaters who fall
Construction zones, intersection debris, fluids and standing water
Road surface hazards include construction zones, other vehicles, debris in intersections, fluids, wet pavement and standing water.
A slick of oil covers part of your lane ahead. What does the chapter say to do?
Slow down and try to avoid driving over it
Brake hard just before you reach the slick
Speed up so that you cross over it quickly
Drive through it with your tires rolling freely
If you spot fluid on the pavement, reduce speed and steer around it rather than through it.
Which hazards does the chapter call especially dangerous when you meet them unexpectedly?
Construction zones, intersection debris and standing water
Potholes, sinkholes, curbs and railroad tracks
Sideswipes, rear-end collisions and head-on collisions
Bushes, small trees, fences and other soft objects
Potholes, sinkholes, curbs and railroad tracks are dangerous, especially when they come up unexpectedly.
A deep pothole appears too late to avoid. How should you take it?
Straight on while braking as hard as you can
At a sharp angle while accelerating through it
At a slight angle with the tires rolling freely
Straight on with all four brakes fully locked
If you cannot avoid an obstacle, hit it at a slight angle with the tires rolling freely.
Your right tires drop off the pavement onto the shoulder. What does the chapter warn against?
Slowing down before steering back
Gripping the wheel firmly
Jerking the wheel to get back on
Steering straight while slowing
If two or more tires drop off the pavement onto an unpaved surface, do not jerk the wheel to get back on; that can flip the vehicle or send it across several lanes.
After two tires leave the pavement, what is the correct recovery?
Slow down, steer straight, then ease back on smoothly
Brake hard, then turn sharply back onto the pavement
Speed up, then steer back while the tires still grip
Stop fully, then reverse slowly back onto the pavement
Instead, ease off the speed and keep the car as straight as the space allows; once you have slowed, hold the wheel firmly and ease the car back onto the pavement in one smooth, steady motion.
What does the chapter say you should anticipate as you look ahead?
When the next shift change is going to come
How much traction your tires will have
How many cars will try to pass you soon
Where the next intersection camera sits
Keep your eyes on the road ahead and predict how much grip the next stretch of pavement will give you.
Why does the chapter tell officers to practice on concrete, gravel, sand and brick?
Those surfaces are where most backing crashes happen
Each of those surfaces needs its own tire PSI setting
Agency policy requires a log of every surface driven
Vehicles respond differently on each surface
Road surfaces include concrete, asphalt, clay, dirt, gravel, sand and brick; vehicles behave differently on each, so practice on each one.
Why must officers learn to drive in all types of weather?
Patrol cars actually handle better in bad weather than in good
Most pursuits in Florida take place during heavy rain storms
They may have to respond during storms others can avoid
Florida law requires every officer to earn a weather certification

Florida weather brings rain, fog, wind and very bright sun; officers may have to drive during heavy storms when others can stay off the road, so they must learn to drive in all weather and know how it affects the vehicle.
Which weather conditions does the chapter say are most likely to affect vehicle performance in Florida?
Rain and wind
Lightning and hail
Fog and smoke
Heat and bright sun
In Florida, rain and wind are the weather conditions most likely to affect vehicle performance.
You just drove through a deep puddle. What does the chapter say often happens to the brakes?
They fade from heat
They pulse under foot
They become wet
They lock up hard
Brakes often get wet when the vehicle goes through deep water or heavy rain.
How much rain does the chapter say can float a car off the road?
Only rain during high wind
Only rain on brick or clay
Only standing water over a foot
Even a small amount
Rain can make a vehicle lose traction and skid out of control, and even a small amount can float a car off the road.
Your tires lose contact with the road on a wet highway and the car pulls left. What is this?
Hydroplaning
The caster effect
Understeer
Wheel tracking
Tires are built to disperse water but can still hydroplane, pulling to one side or not holding at all.
Why does the chapter say to avoid driving through standing water?
It always hides potholes and sinkholes beneath the surface
It may be deeper than it looks and cause mechanical failures
It cools the brakes too quickly and makes them crack
It switches off the anti-lock braking system until it dries
Stay out of water whenever you can: it may be deeper than it appears and can damage the vehicle's mechanical parts.
On a windy night, what does the chapter say strong wind can do besides affect your handling?
Make the six-second following rule no longer necessary
Push other drivers off course and drop limbs or debris
Raise the risk of overdriving your own headlights at night
Increase the caster effect each time you come out of a turn
Strong wind can affect handling, push other drivers off course and bring tree limbs and debris down into your path.
A car pulls out of a driveway directly in front of you, forcing you to swerve. How does the chapter classify crashes like this?
Always preventable by keeping to the three-second rule
Caused mainly by an improper backing maneuver
Always the officer's fault for failing to see the hazard
Sometimes unavoidable because of another driver's actions
Some crashes cannot be prevented, because of what another driver does or because an officer misses a hazard; a car pulling out suddenly and forcing an evasive move is one example.
Where does the chapter say officers face the single greatest threat to safe vehicle operation?
Highway on-ramps
School zones
Intersections
Parking lots
Take special care at intersections, the biggest single threat to operating a vehicle safely.
A car ahead brakes suddenly. Which actions does the chapter list to avoid a crash?
Turn on the emergency lights and accelerate past the car
Ease off the accelerator, use evasive maneuvers or brake
Pull the parking brake hard and steer toward the right
Sound the horn, flash the headlights and hold your lane
Ways to avoid a crash: take your foot off the accelerator to slow down, use evasive maneuvers or brake.
Which steering choice does the chapter call a good crash-avoidance tactic?
Steer to a safe spot in the direction you want to go
Steer toward the hazard so that you keep it in sight
Steer hard to the left into the oncoming traffic lane
Lock the wheel straight ahead and brake as hard as possible
Steering toward a safe spot, in the direction you mean to travel, is another sound way to avoid a crash.
Which kinds of belt does the chapter say count as wearing your seat belt?
A lap belt or a shoulder strap used on its own
Only a harness that the agency has formally approved
A standard lap and chest belt or a tactical harness
Only a lap belt, and only in older patrol vehicles
Always wear your seat belt, whether a standard lap and chest belt or a tactical harness.
Who must wear a safety belt under the Florida Safety Belt Law?
Only drivers who are traveling on highways
Only drivers who are carrying passengers
Every person operating a motor vehicle
Only drivers who are younger than 18
Under the Florida Safety Belt Law (s. 316.614, F.S.), anyone driving a motor vehicle must wear a safety belt.
A 19-year-old rides in your front seat. What does the Florida Safety Belt Law require?
A belt only on highways
No belt, since adults choose for themselves
A safety belt while the vehicle is moving
A belt or child restraint device
Under the Florida Safety Belt Law, a front-seat passenger 18 or older must wear a safety belt while the vehicle is moving.
A 15-year-old rides in your back seat. What does the law require?
A tactical harness like the driver wears
A safety belt or a child restraint device
No restraint at all while in the back seat
A safety belt, but only if seated in front
Under the Florida Safety Belt Law, every driver and passenger under 18 must be restrained by a safety belt or a child restraint device under s. 316.613, F.S.
What does the chapter say about passengers during transport?
Almost all must be belted, and policy mirrors the law
Agency policy overrides the state's seat belt law
Only the passengers in the front seat need belts
None need belts as long as they are in custody
The law has exceptions, but nearly all passengers must be belted during transport, and agency policy follows the law.
A recruit says the airbags will protect him, so he skips his belt. What does the chapter say?
Belts are optional whenever you are driving under 35 mph
Airbags have replaced seat belts in modern patrol vehicles
Belts are a primary safety device; never rely on airbags alone
Belts are required only while driving in emergency mode
The seat belt is a primary safety device; never count on the airbags alone.
A car crosses the center line toward you. Besides reacting, what does the chapter say to do?
Flash your high beams and hold your own lane
Turn on emergency lights and accelerate away
Look for obstacles around you and slow down
Turn left so you pass behind the other car
When a vehicle comes at you in your lane, look around for obstacles while you act to avoid the crash or lessen it, and slow down to buy reaction time.
To avoid a head-on collision, which direction does the chapter say to move?
To the left
Straight ahead while braking
To the right
Into the oncoming lane
Moving right gives the oncoming car more room and sets you up to leave the road; if needed, leaving the road is the final way to escape the crash.
Forced off the road, which of these is the least dangerous to hit?
A parked car
A car moving your way
A road sign
A row of bushes

If you are forced off the road, choose what to hit, from least to most dangerous: soft objects (bushes, small trees, fences), then objects moving your way (including another vehicle), then a fixed object (tree, sign, parked car).
You can't avoid hitting a tree. What part of the car should take the impact?
The rear, after spinning the car
The front corner at full speed
The side, so you glance off
The front, so the airbags deploy
If you cannot avoid a fixed object or an oncoming vehicle, hit it with the side of your vehicle and glance off rather than hitting it head on.
What does the three-second rule establish?
The minimum safe following distance
The time to hold the transmit button
The time to wait at a stop sign
The maximum time to react at night
The three-second rule gives the smallest safe gap behind the car ahead for every vehicle, and with it the space and time to react.
When is the three-second rule meant to be used?
Only during emergency responses to calls
At the posted speed in good conditions
Only when driving through fog or smoke
Only when following other responding units
The three-second rule is meant for the posted speed limit in good weather and road conditions, but you can use it at any speed to check your following distance.
How do you measure following distance with the three-second rule?
Count the number of car lengths between you and it
Count from the moment you see its brake lights come on
Count the seconds until the car ahead changes lanes
Count from when the car ahead passes a fixed point
To use it, note when the vehicle ahead passes a fixed point and count 'one-thousand one, one-thousand two, one-thousand three' until you reach the same point.
You reach the fixed point at the count of two. What does the chapter say to do?
Choose another fixed point and count again
Speed up a little to keep pace with the car
Pass the car ahead on the left when it is safe
Count to six instead from that point onward
If you reach or pass the fixed point before you finish counting three seconds, pick a new point and count again; passing it after three seconds means a safe distance.
Heavy rain is falling. How does your following distance change?
Keep three seconds but slow down
Count six seconds instead of three
Count three seconds but from a closer point
Count four seconds instead of three
In poor road conditions or bad weather use the six-second rule; you count the same way, but count to six once the car ahead passes your fixed point.
You are responding with two other units. Which following rule does the chapter call for?
The two-second rule
The three-second rule
The six-second rule
The one-car-length rule
The six-second rule also applies when driving faster than normal, during emergency responses and when traveling with other responding units.
A recruit asks what a patrol car reacts to. Which answer matches the chapter?
Weather alerts, dispatch calls and the agency's policy
Driver input, road conditions and natural forces
Fuel level, the age of the tires and the engine's size
Speed limits, traffic signals and the other drivers nearby
A vehicle reacts to what the driver does, to the road and to natural forces.
About how big is each tire contact patch on most patrol vehicles?
About 3 inches square
About 12 inches square
About 6 inches square
About 18 inches square
Most patrol vehicles ride on four tire contact patches of about 6 inches square each, and every force acting on the vehicle works through those four small areas.
Which list names the three types of vehicular motion?
Roll, yaw and drift
Yaw, skid and spin
Pitch, roll and sway
Pitch, roll and yaw
The three types of vehicular motion are pitch, roll and yaw.
You brake hard and the nose dips as weight moves forward. Which motion is this?
Pitch
Yaw
Wheel tracking
Roll
Pitch happens when accelerating or braking and moves the vehicle's weight front to rear or rear to front.
Taking a sharp turn, your car leans to the outside as weight shifts sideways. Which motion is this?
Pitch
Understeer
Yaw
Roll
Roll comes with turning and moves the vehicle's weight across from one side to the other.
Your car spins end for end and ends up facing the way you came. Which motion is this?
Oversteer
Roll
Yaw
Pitch
Yaw is a weight transfer that swings the vehicle end for end, turning it 180 degrees on a horizontal plane.
How does a stable vehicle behave compared with an unstable one?
It needs more steering input
It pitches more but rolls less
It yaws more in tight turns
It pitches and rolls less
Stability controls how much a vehicle pitches, rolls and yaws; a stable vehicle pitches and rolls less than an unstable one.
Why are trucks and SUVs less stable than sedans, according to the center-of-gravity rule?
Their tire contact patches are larger
Their tracking width is much wider
Their center of gravity sits lower
Their center of gravity is higher
The most stable vehicle has a low, centered center of gravity; the higher the center of gravity, the lower the stability, which is why trucks and SUVs are less stable.
What does a wider tracking width, like a military Humvee's, do to stability?
Has no effect
Depends on the load
Decreases it
Increases it
A wider tracking width, as on a military Humvee, makes a vehicle more stable; as tracking width shrinks, stability drops, another reason trucks and SUVs are less stable.
In an extreme swerve near the limit of traction, which system helps you keep control?
The caster effect in the steering
The anti-lock braking system
The shuffle steering technique
Electronic stability control
Electronic stability control (ESC) helps the driver keep control during extreme steering, even near or past the limits of road traction.
How does the chapter describe the traction control system?
A primary function of the braking system
A feature built only into trucks and SUVs
Usually a secondary function of ESC
A full replacement for the ABS system
A traction control system (TCS) is usually a secondary function of ESC and is designed to prevent loss of traction.
You load heavy gear in the trunk and a partner in the front. What does the chapter tell you about loading?
Keep the trunk empty
Raise the tire PSI above the doorjamb
Put the heaviest gear in front
Distribute the weight evenly
The gear and people a car carries change how weight transfers and can alter its stability, so load equipment so the weight is spread evenly.
Where is a vehicle's weight carried, according to the chapter?
Mostly on the rear axle and rear tires
Evenly across the whole length of the frame
Mostly at the vehicle's center of gravity
Only where the tires touch the road
Weight transfer and distribution happen when speed changes and affect handling; weight is carried only where the tires touch the road.
You slam the brake instead of easing it. What does the chapter say happens to weight transfer?
It shifts toward the rear
It becomes more dramatic
It stays exactly the same
It disappears completely
The harder you hit the brake or the gas pedal, the bigger the weight shift and its effect on the car.
Braking shifts weight in the direction of travel. What does that transfer affect?
Fuel economy
Headlight aim
Stopping distance
Radio range
Braking shifts weight in the direction of travel, forward or backward, which affects stopping distance.
When you accelerate, where does the weight go?
To the rear tires
To the inside tires
To the outside tires
To the front tires
Accelerating shifts weight to the rear tires, which affects acceleration and handling; weight also transfers when the vehicle changes direction.
Why does the chapter warn that weight transfer in a turn is more noticeable in a van, truck or SUV than in a sedan?
It can push the car out of its lane or roll it
It throws glare that blinds oncoming drivers
It makes the brakes fade faster on long drives
It locks the rear wheels in the middle of a turn
In a turn, weight moves across the car, and you feel it more in a van, truck or SUV than in a sedan; it can carry the car out of its lane or off the road and, at worst, roll it over.
In a right turn, which wheel carries the most weight?
The rear left wheel
The front left wheel
The rear right wheel
The front right wheel
When turning, weight shifts toward the outside tires: the front outside wheel carries the most, then the rear outside wheel, then the front inside wheel, and the rear inside wheel the least.
Because steering ability drops in a turn, what does the chapter tell you to do?
Brake before the turn, then steer
Brake and steer at the same time
Accelerate through the whole turn
Steer first, then brake in the turn
Because steering ability is reduced in a turn, do not brake and steer at the same time: brake before the turn, then steer into it.
How does the chapter define a radius?
The distance from a circle's center to its edge
The width between a vehicle's left and right wheels
The center point of any curve in the road
The tighter path that the rear wheels follow
A radius is the distance from a circle's center to its edge, and every turn or curve is part of a circle.
A highway ramp gets wider the further you go around it. What kind of turn is it?
A decreasing radius
A constant radius
An increasing radius
An early apex turn
An increasing radius turn widens as you go through it, like a circle growing larger.
A curve tightens the further you drive into it. What kind of turn is it?
A late apex
A decreasing radius
An increasing radius
A constant radius
A decreasing radius turn tightens as you go through it, like a circle getting smaller.
Which example does the chapter give of a constant radius turn?
A long, sweeping highway on-ramp
A three-point U-turn done in reverse
A 90-degree turn at an intersection
A cloverleaf exit off an interstate
A constant radius turn stays the same the whole way, neither widening nor tightening; a 90-degree turn at an intersection is an example.
What does a tight turn require to get through safely?
Less speed and less steering input
A constant speed and no braking at all
Less speed and more steering input
More speed and less steering input
A tight turn needs less speed and more steering input to get through safely.
Where is the apex of a curve?
At its widest edge
At its very entry
At its center point
At its very exit
The apex is the midpoint of a curve.
What defines whether you are using an early, center or late apex?
How hard you brake in the curve itself
Your position relative to the curve
Your speed as you enter the curve
Which of your hands is at 12 o'clock
Apexing is how you steer the vehicle in relation to the curve's apex while staying in your lane; your position relative to the curve defines early, center or late apexing.
You start turning the moment the curve begins and reach the inside before the apex. Which technique is this?
Late apex
Constant radius
Center apex
Early apex
In early apexing the car comes nearest the inside edge before it reaches the apex, because the turn starts right at the beginning of the curve.
What risk does early apexing create?
It pushes the car outward and can cause loss of control
It leaves the most room for driver error in the curve
It reduces the outward force acting on the moving car
It makes the rear wheels track a wider path than the front
Early apexing increases the force pushing the vehicle outward, away from the curve's center, and can cause loss of control.
You drive moderately into the curve and come closest to the inside at its middle. Which technique is this?
Center apex
Late apex
Decreasing radius
Early apex
In center apexing the car is nearest the inside at the curve's midpoint; you drive part way into the curve before turning.
You drive deep into the curve before turning and pass closest to the inside after the apex. Which technique is this?
Late apex
Early apex
Increasing radius
Center apex
In late apexing the car reaches the inside edge only after passing the apex; you drive deep into the curve before turning.
Which apexing technique does the chapter call best in most cases?
Center apex, because it splits the difference between them
Early apex, because it reduces the outward force on the car
Early apex, because it starts the turn sooner in the curve
Late apex, because it leaves the most room for error
Late apexing reduces the outward force on the vehicle and the chance of losing control; in most cases it is the best cornering method and leaves the most room for driver error.
Where do all three apexing techniques finish the turn?
Along the outside edge of your lane
In the center of the neighboring lane
Along the inside edge of your lane
On the paved shoulder past the curve
With every apexing technique you finish the turn along the outside edge of your lane.
Which two things does the chapter say most influence steering-related forces?
Hand position and the height of the seat
Tire PSI and the level of every fluid
Mirror angle and the darkness of the tint
Speed and how forcefully you steer
Steering is directly tied to vehicle dynamics, handling and traction control, and speed and how forcefully you steer shape those forces and the weight transfer that affects control.
What causes understeer and oversteer?
A low level of power steering fluid
Turning the steering wheel too far each way
A faulty or worn-out steering column
The front or rear tires losing traction

Understeer and oversteer describe movements caused by the front or rear tires losing traction; the word steer in them does not mean turning the steering wheel, though recovering may take steering input.
In a curve, your car turns less sharply than you meant. What is it?
Understeer
Yaw
Oversteer
Wheel tracking
Understeer is when the vehicle turns less sharply than the driver intends.
Which combination of errors does the chapter say can cause understeer?
Low tire PSI, tread worn to the wear bars and brakes that got wet
Excess speed, poor front traction and improper braking in a turn
High speed, the rear tires losing grip and heavy braking in a turn
Braking too late, apexing too early and gripping the wheel tightly
Understeer can come from too much speed, too little grip on the front (steering) tires and braking wrongly in a turn; two or more of these together can make you lose control.
Understeer sets in mid-curve. What is the correction?
Release the wheel and let the car straighten itself
Off the accelerator, keep steering input, do not brake
Brake hard and turn the steering wheel even further
Accelerate to put more weight on the front tires
To correct understeer, take your foot off the accelerator, keep your steering input without braking and, if needed, steer to a safe place and stop.
Your car turns sharper than you meant and the rear swings out. What is it?
Pitch
Roll
Understeer
Oversteer
Oversteer is when the vehicle turns more sharply than the driver intends, sometimes with the rear sliding out.
When does oversteer usually happen?
When you use shuffle steering while driving in reverse
At low speed when the front tires lose their grip in a curve
At higher speed when the rear tires lose grip under heavy braking
When you hold a constant speed as you enter the turn
Oversteer usually happens at higher speed when the rear tires lose their grip and the driver brakes too hard in a turn or curve.
How do you correct oversteer?
Off the gas or brake, steer where you want, no brakes
Brake hard and steer the car straight ahead at once
Accelerate hard and turn the wheel away from the slide
Release the wheel and pull the parking brake to stop
To correct oversteer, take your foot off the accelerator or brake, steer where you want to go (if the front tires still have traction), do not brake and, if needed, steer to a safe place and stop.
In a turn, how does the rear wheels' path compare with the front wheels' path?
Both follow the same path
The rear wheels follow a tighter path
The rear wheels follow the outside edge
The rear wheels follow a wider path
Wheel tracking means the rear wheels follow a tighter path than the front wheels in a turn.
You must steer around a parked car close to your right. Where do you aim the front of your car?
Straight, then swerve after passing it
Wide of the car, so the rear wheels clear it
Close to it, since the rear follows the front
Right at its corner, then turn away
To avoid a fixed object, steer the front of the vehicle wide of it so the rear wheels do not hit it.
Why does the chapter say how you sit matters?
It lets you steer, accelerate, use mirrors and brake correctly
It sets the size of the tire contact patch under each wheel
It reduces the glare you get from oncoming headlights
It keeps the airbag in the wheel from deploying in a crash
How you sit lets you steer, accelerate, use the mirrors, keep the right seat position and brake correctly.
A recruit white-knuckles the wheel through the course. What does the chapter warn?
A tight grip weakens the car's caster effect
Gripping too tightly tires you more quickly
A tight grip sets off the anti-lock brakes
A tight grip is required at 4 and 8 o'clock
Grip the wheel firmly but relaxed with your thumbs resting on the rim; holding it too tightly tires you faster.
When should you use proper hand position and grip?
Only while driving on the training range
Only when you are driving above 35 mph
Every time you take control of a vehicle
Only during emergency responses and pursuits
Use proper hand position and grip every time you take control of a vehicle.
Facing the wheel, which positions mark top center and bottom center?
12 o'clock and 6 o'clock
10 o'clock and 2 o'clock
4 o'clock and 8 o'clock
9 o'clock and 3 o'clock
On the steering wheel, top center is the 12 o'clock position and bottom center is 6 o'clock.
Where does the chapter recommend you place your hands?
Right hand at 2, left hand at 10
Right hand at 8, left hand at 4
Right hand at 3, left hand at 9
Right hand at 4, left hand at 8
The recommended hand position is the right hand at 4 o'clock and the left hand at 8 o'clock; some wheel designs need a slightly different position.
Which benefits does the 4 and 8 o'clock position give?
Better mirror view, less glare and less road noise
A tighter grip, more control and faster braking
Quicker response, less fatigue and less airbag injury
More caster effect, less wheel spin and less body roll
Holding at 4 and 8 o'clock lets you react faster, tires you less and lowers the chance of injury if the airbag goes off.
When does the chapter say shuffle steering is not used?
When driving in reverse
When making a left turn
When driving above 35 mph
When the caster effect occurs
After adjusting the equipment, put your hands in position and grip the wheel; use shuffle steering for right and left turns, but not when driving in reverse.
To start a right turn with shuffle steering, which hand goes to 12 o'clock?
The left hand
Both hands together
The right hand
Neither of the hands
To start a right turn with shuffle steering, move the right hand up to 12 o'clock and pull the wheel down smoothly.
In a right turn, after the right hand pulls down from 12, what does the left hand do?
Crosses over to the right side of the wheel
Moves up to the 12 o'clock position as well
Slides down to 6 o'clock, keeping contact
Lets go of the wheel until the turn is done
Right turn step 1: keeping contact with the wheel, slide the left hand down to 6 o'clock.
When your hands meet at 6 o'clock in a right turn, what happens?
The left hand grips and the right loosens but keeps contact
Both hands release together and the wheel spins back freely
The right hand grips firmly and the left hand lets go of the wheel
Both hands grip together and pull the wheel down as one

Right turn step 2: as the hands meet at 6 o'clock, grip with the left hand and loosen the right while keeping it in contact, shuffling the wheel hand to hand as the left hand rotates up toward 12 o'clock.
What is the third step of a right-turn shuffle?
The right hand slides back up to 12 o'clock
The right hand crosses over to the left side
The left hand slides down to 6 o'clock again
Both hands return to the 4 and 8 positions
Right turn step 3: keeping contact with the wheel, slide the right hand up to 12 o'clock.
Which rule holds throughout shuffle steering?
Both hands stay fixed at 4 and 8 o'clock
The left hand always stays at 12 o'clock
Neither hand crosses 12 or 6 o'clock
One hand always leaves the wheel at the top
During shuffle steering, no hand crosses over the top (12 o'clock) or under the bottom (6 o'clock); each hand stays on its own half of the wheel.
Why does the chapter call shuffle steering imperative?
It keeps the airbag in the steering wheel from deploying
It is the only safe way to steer while driving in reverse
It keeps control of the wheel when the caster effect occurs
It stops the rear wheels from tracking a tighter path
Shuffle steering is essential because it keeps control of the wheel, especially when the caster effect happens.
Coming out of a turn, you relax your grip and the wheel straightens on its own. What is this?
Understeer
Wheel tracking
The caster effect
Optical driving
The caster effect is a forward-moving vehicle's tendency to straighten out of a turn when the driver releases the wheel; shuffle steering lets it work for you, and it does not apply in reverse.
A deer appears on the left shoulder. Where does optical driving tell you to look?
In the rearview mirror
Where you want the car to go
At the deer, to judge its path
At the speedometer
Optical driving, also called eye-targeting, means looking where you want to go to avoid an obstacle so you do not steer toward it.
What is proper braking, according to the chapter?
Pressing the pedal with steadily increasing pressure
Pumping the brake pedal in short, quick bursts
Pressing hard all at once and holding it there
Easing off and back onto the pedal to avoid a skid
Correct braking means pushing the pedal with steadily rising pressure to slow or stop in the least time.
What is the first step of proper braking?
Release the accelerator and coast
Lift the right foot and press the brake with the toes
Press the brake with the left foot
Pivot the right foot to the brake, heel on the floor
Braking step 1: pivot your right foot from the gas pedal to the brake, keeping your heel on the floor.
Where does the ball of the right foot go when braking?
The right edge of the brake pedal
The left edge of the brake pedal
The base of the accelerator
The center of the brake pedal
Braking step 2: set the ball of your right foot in the middle of the brake pedal.
What does the anti-lock braking system do?
Keeps the wheels from locking so you can still steer
Locks the rear wheels on purpose to prevent a spin
Stops the tires from spinning when you accelerate
Straightens the car on its own after you finish a turn
Anti-lock brakes (ABS) now come standard; the system stops the wheels from locking by pulsing the brake on and off very fast, so the driver can still steer.
When do ABS and non-ABS brakes behave differently?
In a hard or sudden emergency stop
Under normal, gradual, everyday braking
Only when the car is driving in reverse
Only on wet roads after a heavy rain
ABS and non-ABS brakes work the same under normal, gradual braking; they behave differently only in a hard or sudden emergency stop.
You need to stop an ABS-equipped car fast. What does the chapter say to do?
Brake lightly and steer away
Brake hard to engage the ABS
Pump the brake to avoid locking
Pull the parking brake
With steady downward pressure on the pedal, the computerized ABS slows and stops the vehicle; to stop quickly, brake hard to engage it.
During a hard stop, the brake pedal pulses under your foot. What does it mean?
One of the rear tires has failed under you
The car is in ABS mode, which is normal
The brake fluid has dropped to a low level
The brakes are fading from too much heat
A pulsing brake pedal is normal and means the vehicle is in ABS mode.
What are the two goals of proper acceleration?
Save fuel and keep the engine noise down
Keep both the caster effect and wheel tracking low
Reach 35 mph quickly and then hold that speed
Avoid losing traction and control weight transfer
Proper acceleration avoids loss of traction and controls weight transfer.
How do you set your foot before accelerating?
Toes on the pedal, with the heel lifted off the floor
Heel at the base of the pedal, ball of the foot on it
Heel resting on the brake, toes on the accelerator
The whole foot laid flat across both of the pedals
Acceleration steps 1 and 2: set your right heel at the foot of the gas pedal and the ball of your foot flat on it.
How should pressure be applied to the accelerator?
Hard enough that the tires spin briefly before they grip
Quickly all the way to the floor, then eased off again
Smoothly and steadily until you reach the rate you want
In short pulses so you can test how much traction you have
Acceleration steps 3 and 4: press the pedal down with the ball of the foot, using smooth, steady pressure until you reach the acceleration rate you want.
Pulling away, your tires start to spin. What do you do?
Press the pedal harder so the tires break through the spin
Release the accelerator at once, then reapply smoothly
Turn the steering wheel side to side to find traction
Brake hard right away so that the spinning stops
Accelerate smoothly in a straight line with steady pressure; if the tires start to spin, release the accelerator at once to stop the spin, then smoothly reapply it.
What does cornering mean in this chapter?
Taking a long highway curve at the posted speed limit
Entering an intersection at normal speed and turning 90 degrees
Turning the car a full 180 degrees in one motion
Backing around a corner on the Tactical Backing course
Cornering means entering an intersection safely at normal speed and making a 90-degree turn right or left; proper braking matters, as does finding the apex and using all the space available.
What keeps a vehicle from traveling in a straight line, according to the cornering lesson?
Holding a constant speed into the turn
Steering input at the wrong speed
Braking to a safe speed before the turn
Feeding the wheel with shuffle steering
Steering input at the wrong speed keeps a vehicle from traveling in a straight line.
Approaching the cornering exercise, what speed do you reach and hold?
45 mph
35 mph
55 mph
25 mph
Cornering steps 1 to 3: drive straight toward the turn, reach and hold 35 mph, and signal before the turn.
When is braking finished in the cornering steps?
At the apex, when the car is nearest the inside
As you exit the curve and begin to straighten
Before the turn, while still driving straight
Midway through the turn, as the car leans
Cornering step 4: brake to a safe speed before the turn and finish braking while still driving straight.
Before the turn, where do you line up?
On the paved shoulder beside the lane
In the very center of the intersection
In the proper lane on the outside of the turn
Along the inside edge of your own lane
Cornering steps 5 and 6: line up in the proper lane on the outside of the turn and pick the apex or path through it.
Why do you hold a constant speed while entering the turn?
So you can count three seconds
So the ABS stays engaged
So the caster effect does not occur
So the weight transfers steadily
Cornering step 7: hold a constant speed as you enter the turn so the weight transfers steadily.
Why does the chapter call backing safely an officer safety skill?
Backing is required in every pursuit
Backing replaces the cornering exercise
Many crashes happen while backing
Backing is graded in every inspection
Many crashes happen while backing, and backing safely is an officer safety skill; improper backing can hit a person or object.
What causes the majority of law enforcement vehicle crashes?
Sideswipes during pursuits
Head-on collisions
Right-angle collisions at intersections
Backing into a fixed object
Most law enforcement vehicle crashes come from backing into a fixed object.
Your car has poor rear visibility. What does the chapter suggest?
Ask a passerby on the sidewalk to guide you back
Rely only on the rearview mirror inside the car
Use the side mirrors or an installed backup camera
Back up quickly so you spend less time in reverse
Some vehicles have poor rear visibility, so use the side mirrors or a backup camera as needed.
Why should you drive slowly in reverse?
The caster effect pulls the car off course in reverse
Shuffle steering is not allowed while backing up
Weight transfer rises and your field of vision shrinks
The anti-lock braking system does not work in reverse
Vehicle dynamics apply in every direction; drive slowly in reverse to make up for more weight transfer and a smaller field of vision.
Why is stopping harder while backing?
The rear brakes are less efficient than the front
The brake pedal travels farther while in reverse
The ABS switches itself off while in reverse
The front brakes tend to lock up when backing
In reverse the rear brakes take much of the weight transfer, yet they are weaker than the front brakes, so stopping while backing is much harder.
On the Reverse Serpentine course, what do you notice about steering?
Large inputs are needed to turn the car at all
Shuffle steering keeps the car smooth and steady
The caster effect straightens the car for you
Small inputs make big changes in direction
In reverse, a little steering input makes a big change in direction, which shows on the Reverse Serpentine course.
On the Tactical Backing course, what can large or quick steering movements do?
Trigger the caster effect
Cause you to lose control
Improve your field of vision
Engage the ABS
Big or quick steering movements in reverse can cost you control, which shows on the Tactical Backing course.
After shifting into reverse, how do you position your body?
Turn left and rest the left arm out the open window
Turn right with the right arm over the passenger seat
Face forward and watch only the mirrors and camera
Turn right but keep both of your hands on the wheel
Backing steps 1 and 2: keep your right foot on the brake as you shift into reverse, then twist your upper body to the right and lay your right arm across the top of the passenger seat.
After turning your body, where do you look?
Down at the gear selector to confirm reverse
At the backup camera screen and nothing else
In the driver's side mirror and nowhere else
Through the rear window, scanning behind the car
Backing step 3: look through the rear window and scan the area behind the vehicle.
When is it acceptable to back up quickly?
Never, under any circumstances
Only in an emergency
Whenever a backup camera is installed
Whenever the area behind is clear
Mirrors are an option when backing, and you should always back slowly except in an emergency.
How does night driving compare with fatal crashes, according to the chapter?
About a third of driving, but over half of fatal crashes
About a third of driving, and a third of fatal crashes
About a quarter of driving, but a third of fatal crashes
About half of all driving, and half of all fatal crashes
Only about one-third of driving happens at night, yet more than half of fatal crashes happen in darkness.
Why are night crashes so deadly, according to the chapter?
Streetlights throw off drivers' depth perception
Most drivers on the road at night are impaired
Drivers keep daytime speeds with less visibility
Emergency lights blind the other drivers on the road
Night crashes are high because drivers think they can drive as fast as in daylight; that false confidence plus reduced visibility makes night driving more dangerous.
What is the most common night driving error?
Overdriving the headlights
Using low beams on dark roads
Dimming lights for oncoming traffic
Looking at the road's shoulder
The most common night driving error is overdriving the headlights: going so fast you cannot stop inside the distance they light.
Under s. 316.237, F.S., how far should high and low beams reveal a person?
450 feet on high, 250 feet on low
450 feet on high, 150 feet on low
500 feet on high, 250 feet on low
350 feet on high, 100 feet on low
Florida law (s. 316.237, F.S.) says high beams should light up a person at 450 feet and low beams at 150 feet.
When does overdriving the headlights matter most?
During shift change at dusk, when the light is fading fast
When the car is parked over grass with the engine running
When backing out of a driveway on a dark residential street
In emergency mode, when speed lengthens stopping distance
Overdriving the headlights matters most in emergency mode, because higher speed lengthens stopping distance and cuts reaction time.
How does darkness affect reaction?
Reaction time holds steady, but spotting a hazard takes longer
Darkness has no effect at all on reaction distance
Reaction time roughly doubles once the sun goes down
Reaction time shortens because the eyes become more alert
Reaction time is the same day or night, but darkness lengthens the time it takes to first see a hazard.
What happens to your field of vision at night?
Side vision widens to make up for the darkness
Depth perception improves as the eyes adjust
Color vision becomes sharper under streetlights
Side vision shrinks and the whole view narrows
At night peripheral vision decreases and less light narrows the field of vision.
Why is it harder to judge oncoming traffic at night?
Many visual cues are lost
Headlights hide road signs
Glare improves distance judgment
Night vision speeds up depth perception
Darkness hides many of the cues you rely on by day, so judging distance and how fast oncoming cars are moving gets harder.
An oncoming truck's lights blind you for a moment. Why?
Eyes adjusted to darkness need time to readjust
Your own interior lights reflect off the windshield
The truck's high beams reach farther than 450 feet
Your emergency lights are reflecting off nearby objects
Glare from oncoming vehicles or other lights can briefly blind a driver, because eyes adjusted to darkness need time to readjust when light changes suddenly.
Why can emergency lights make night driving harder?
They cause other drivers to pull to the left instead
They cut the reach of your headlights in half at night
They drain the battery and make the headlights go dim
Their high intensity reflects off objects and adds glare
In emergency mode the emergency lights add glare, because their high intensity reflects easily off objects.
An oncoming car approaches with bright lights. What does the chapter say to do first?
Speed up so that you pass the oncoming car more quickly
Turn on your interior dome light to see the road better
Reduce speed and avoid looking straight at the lights
Flash your own high beams back at the oncoming car
Slow down and do not look straight into oncoming headlights.
Where do you look to protect your night vision from oncoming headlights?
Toward the shoulder, using the white edge line
Straight at the oncoming headlights to judge them
At your speedometer until the car has passed
At the center line, to keep the lane in view
Look toward the shoulder and use the white edge line for guidance to protect your night vision.
Why dim your headlights for oncoming traffic?
To meet the 150-foot low-beam standard in the statute
To cut glare and protect other drivers' night vision
To save battery power for the radio and light bar
To avoid overdriving your own headlights at night
Dim your headlights for oncoming traffic to cut glare and protect other drivers' night vision.
Smoke drifts across the road in daylight. Which beams does the chapter say to use?
Emergency lights only
No headlights in daylight
Low beams
High beams
Use low beams in fog or smoke, day or night, to limit the glare reflected back at you.
Your laptop and dome light are bright while you drive at night. What does the chapter say?
Leave them on so that they keep you alert
Turn them up to balance out the outside glare
Use them to help light up the road's edge
Control all interior lights to reduce glare
Control all interior lights to reduce glare.
How does the chapter describe the decision to drive in emergency mode?
One left entirely up to the dispatcher
One made only by an on-duty supervisor
One that must never be taken lightly
One required for every priority call
The decision to drive in emergency mode must never be taken lightly; it puts you and the public at risk.
Why are emergency responses and pursuits among the most dangerous driving situations?
Emergency vehicles have weaker brakes than other cars do
Sirens confuse the other emergency units on the road
Officers may feel psychological and physiological effects
Most of them take place in fog or heavy smoke
Emergency responses and pursuits are among the most dangerous driving situations because of the psychological and physiological effects officers may experience.
Florida law sets rules for emergency vehicles, and your agency adds more limits. Which do you follow?
State law only, because it always overrides policy
The dispatcher's instructions, over law and policy
Whichever of the two rules is less restrictive
Your agency's policy, which can add restrictions
You must follow Florida law on emergency vehicles, and agency policy can add more limits on when and how you drive in emergency mode; fall back on your agency's policy.
How does the chapter suggest you stay current on emergency-driving law?
Follow the most recent local news reports
Consult supervisors and your agency's legal advisers
Ask the public safety telecommunicator on duty
Read through every new statute each January
Court decisions and new laws keep changing the rules, so check with supervisors and agency legal advisers to stay current.
What allows a response to be both rapid and safe?
Following the first unit as closely as possible
Running the siren continuously the whole way
Driving at least 20 miles over the limit
Good judgment and good driving technique
Once in emergency mode, stay focused on safety; always control the vehicle with proper steering, braking and acceleration, since good judgment and technique allow a fast and safe response.
A rookie is determined to beat every other unit to a call. What stress does the chapter describe?
Time distortion that makes the whole drive seem very short
Selective hearing that blocks out the radio traffic entirely
Tunnel vision that narrows your view of the road ahead
Pushing past your own or the car's limits to arrive first
The stress of an emergency call can tempt you past what you or the car can handle, chasing the violator no matter what or racing to arrive first.
Once you know the physiological effects of emergency mode, what does the chapter tell you to do?
Turn off the siren so you can calm down
Keep them under control while responding
Drive with the window up to help you focus
Hand the call off to another nearby unit
Know these body reactions and keep them in check whenever you respond in emergency mode.
Who does the chapter say is responsible for a safe emergency response?
The dispatcher
The other drivers on the road
Your supervisor
You, the driving officer
Use every piece of emergency equipment you have, and use it correctly; a safe response is your responsibility.
At 3 a.m. you wonder whether lights and siren will wake the neighborhood. What should decide it?
The time of night
How busy the road is
The needs of the call
Whether drivers will be inconvenienced
Decide on lights based on what the call needs, not on outside concerns such as waking people at night or inconveniencing other drivers.
Why does the chapter say a siren is not a protective shield?
Sirens make the six-second rule unnecessary in traffic
Sirens drain the car's battery during long responses
Sirens are illegal in residential areas late at night
Many drivers can't hear it with windows up and radios on
A siren is not a protective shield: drivers with radios and air conditioning on, windows up or soundproof cars may not hear it.
Approaching a red light in emergency mode, what does the chapter tell you to do?
Yield or stop as needed and make eye contact with drivers
Turn off your lights so the waiting drivers stay calm
Proceed at full speed, since you have the right-of-way
Use the opposite lane to bypass the traffic that is stopped
Approach intersections correctly, yielding or stopping when needed, to show due regard for others' safety when asking for the right-of-way, and make eye contact with drivers there when you can.
Why keep a proper following distance in emergency mode?
