It protects the strength of your radio signal
It lets the anti-lock brakes work the way they should
The driver ahead may not see your lights if you are close
It keeps your siren from echoing off the car ahead
Leave a proper gap behind both civilian cars and other emergency vehicles; if you ride too close, the driver ahead may never see your lights in the mirror.
Where does the chapter tell you to position your car in emergency mode?
Offset to the left, inside your lane
Straddling the center line of the road
Centered exactly in the middle of your lane
Offset to the right, out on the shoulder
Keep your car toward the left of the road while staying in your lane, so the cars ahead and oncoming drivers can see you, ideally in both the rearview and side mirrors of the car in front.
Who must you stay in contact with while driving in emergency mode?
The violator, over your car's loudspeaker
Your supervisor, and only your supervisor
The dispatcher and other responding units
The receiving hospital and fire rescue
Stay in contact with the dispatcher and the other responding units while in emergency mode.
The fleeing driver starts weaving through traffic at 90 mph. What does the chapter say about your own driving?
Never let the violator's driving dictate your own
Copy the violator's route exactly so you stay close
Drive ahead of the violator so you can cut him off
Match the violator's speed so that you don't lose him
A pursuit aims to catch a fleeing violator; you cannot steer the violator's driving or route, so never let how the violator drives decide how you drive.
What does an officer weigh in deciding whether to start a pursuit?
Whether the violator's car has been reported as stolen
Whether officers from other agencies are already pursuing
How fast the patrol car is compared with the violator's car
The risks to themselves and the public against the benefit
Deciding to start a pursuit depends on knowing agency policy and Florida law and on the conditions at the time; weigh the risks to you and the public against the benefit of the arrest.
Which situation fits the chapter's definition of a pursuit?
You drive in emergency mode to reach a crash with injuries
You park your patrol car across a road to block the traffic
Your emergency equipment is on and the driver speeds up to escape
You follow a speeding car without lights so you can read its tag

A pursuit is an active attempt, in an authorized emergency vehicle with its emergency equipment on, to apprehend the occupants of a moving vehicle whose driver speeds up, takes other evasive action or refuses to stop to avoid capture.
Besides starting, what does the chapter say you must consider about a pursuit?
The cost of the fuel and wear on the patrol vehicle
The amount of overtime that the pursuit will create
What ending it means if the violator keeps driving recklessly
The media attention the pursuit may draw afterward
Consider the decision to engage and the consequences of starting and ending a pursuit, especially if the violator keeps driving recklessly afterward.
What did the U.S. Supreme Court hold in DeShaney v. Winnebago County?
No duty to guarantee safety unless a special relationship exists
Every decision to pursue is reviewed under the doctrine of negligence
Every roadblock must give the violator enough time to stop
Officers must guarantee everyone's safety during every pursuit

In DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services (1989), the U.S. Supreme Court held that officers and agencies do not have to guarantee anyone's safety unless a special relationship exists.
When does a special relationship arise under DeShaney?
When an officer first begins a pursuit of a fleeing vehicle
When law enforcement restricts a person's freedom, as in custody
When a citizen calls 911 and asks the police for help
When an officer turns on the emergency lights and the siren

A special relationship exists, for example, with a person in custody: once law enforcement restricts someone's freedom of movement, it is responsible for keeping that person reasonably free from harm.
You end a pursuit, and the violator later crashes into a parked car. What does the chapter say about your liability?
You are liable unless a supervisor ordered the end
You are liable because you started the pursuit
You are liable if the crash happens within a mile
You are unlikely to be liable
Starting a pursuit does not create a duty to continue it, and an officer who ends a pursuit is unlikely to be liable if the violator keeps driving recklessly.
What did City of Pinellas Park v. Brown hold?
Officers are liable only if their actions shock the conscience
Only the reasonableness of the officers' actions matters
Continuing a pursuit carries a duty to protect the public
Officers owe no duty unless the person is in their custody
City of Pinellas Park v. Brown (Fla. 1992) holds that when officers choose to keep a pursuit going, they owe the public a duty of protection.
In the Pinellas Park pursuit, how many vehicles were involved and what did the officers do wrong?
About 15 vehicles, using a PIT at a very high speed
About 25 vehicles, chasing a stolen 18-wheeler truck
About 15 vehicles, all continuing against department policy
About 5 vehicles, using a roadblock set up around a curve
In the Pinellas Park case, about 15 vehicles from three jurisdictions joined a pursuit on a main road, and every officer and deputy broke department policy by continuing it.
How did the two sisters die in the Pinellas Park case?
They were riding as passengers in the fleeing driver's car
A patrol car rammed their car by mistake during the pursuit
They pulled out on a green light into the fleeing car's path
Their car struck a roadblock that was set around a curve

In Pinellas Park, an officer in an unmarked car pulled out from a side street to get ahead of the pursuit; two sisters waiting to cross pulled into the fleeing car's path on a green light, and both sisters and the fleeing driver died.
What did the Florida Supreme Court find about the officers' actions in Pinellas Park?
They created a special relationship with the two sisters
They were so extreme that they shocked the conscience
They were reasonable under the Fourth Amendment
They created a risk that was foreseeable and preventable
The Florida Supreme Court found the law enforcement action created a foreseeable and preventable risk to the public.
Under Pinellas Park, how can a decision to start or continue a pursuit be reviewed?
Under the doctrine of negligence, not only as force
It cannot be reviewed by any court at all
Only as a use of force under the Fourth Amendment
Only under the shock-the-conscience standard
The court did not ban pursuits, but any decision to start or continue one can be reviewed under the doctrine of negligence, not only as a Fourth Amendment use of force.
When law enforcement owes a person a duty of care and its action injures that person, what must the court decide?
Whether the person was in custody
Whether officers acted reasonably
Whether the officers intended harm
Whether officers used a roadblock
When law enforcement owes a resident a duty of care and its action or inaction injures or kills that person, the court decides whether law enforcement acted reasonably.
Your sergeant tells you to let a fleeing car go. What did the Florida Supreme Court note about losing a vehicle?
The agency must set up a roadblock in its place
The violator can often be identified and caught later
The officer who ended it becomes liable for later crashes
Losing the car means the case is closed for good
The court also noted that losing a vehicle in a pursuit does not mean it will never be found; it is not 'now or never,' and a violator can be identified and arrested later.
What does the chapter call the best way to avoid liability in a pursuit?
Keeping the violator in sight at all costs
Using a PIT as early as possible
Letting dispatch make every decision
Following your agency's policies
Sticking to agency policy is the surest way to stay clear of liability in a pursuit.
What did Brower v. County of Inyo hold about some pursuit tactics?
They are always protected as reasonable by the courts
They are reviewed only under the doctrine of negligence
They can be an unconstitutional seizure by deadly force
They are banned outright in every state in the country
In Brower v. County of Inyo (1989), the U.S. Supreme Court held that some pursuit tactics can lead to a claim of an unconstitutional seizure by deadly force.
What did officers do in Brower v. County of Inyo?
Rammed the fleeing car with three marked patrol cars in a row
Hid an 18-wheeler around a curve and aimed headlights at the driver
Used a PIT at a much higher speed than their training allowed
Pulled out from a side street to get ahead of the pursuit
In Brower, officers parked an 18-wheeler around a curve as a roadblock and aimed a police car's headlights to blind the driver; he hit the truck and died.
Which earlier deadly force case did the Court rely on in Brower?
Tennessee v. Garner
DeShaney v. Winnebago County
County of Sacramento v. Lewis
Scott v. Harris
Brower relied heavily on Tennessee v. Garner (1985), which concerned deadly force against a person for a non-dangerous crime, and separated pursuing a person from blocking or seizing them.
In Brower and Garner, what did the Court say about deadly force?
It is allowed any time a driver flees from the police
It is judged only under the doctrine of negligence
It is allowed once the violator is taken into custody
It should not be used to catch people for minor offenses
In both Brower and Garner, the Court said deadly force is not for catching people who commit minor offenses such as traffic violations.
When do officers become responsible for a fleeing violator's injury or death?
Whenever they begin a pursuit of a vehicle that will not stop
When they force a stop, such as by roadblock or vehicle contact
Whenever the violator is driving recklessly during the chase
Whenever the pursuit goes on for more than a few minutes

Merely pursuing creates no special relationship, so officers are not responsible for the violator's injury or death; but forcing a stop by roadblock or vehicle contact makes officers responsible for the results, because it becomes a Fourth Amendment seizure.
What does the chapter say happens when an officer intentionally uses a patrol car as a weapon?
It becomes a deadly weapon governed by use of force policy
It is treated as one more routine pursuit tactic
It is reviewed only by the dispatcher on duty
It is allowed as long as the violator is a felon
A patrol car used on purpose as a weapon is a deadly weapon, covered by agency use of force policy like any weapon of opportunity, and that includes tactics such as ramming.
What standard did County of Sacramento v. Lewis adopt for officer liability?
Reasonableness alone
Simple negligence
Deliberate indifference
Shocking the conscience

In County of Sacramento v. Lewis (1998), the U.S. Supreme Court held that officers may be liable for injury or death from a pursuit or emergency response if their actions 'shock the conscience,' decided case by case.
Under Lewis, what must a pursuing officer have done to shock the conscience?
Ignored the agency's written policy on the length of pursuits
Driven carelessly or negligently during the high-speed pursuit
Intended harm to the violator without justification for deadly force
Failed to tell dispatch that the pursuit had started or ended

Lewis separated mere carelessness or negligence, deliberate indifference and intent to harm; in a high-speed pursuit, shocking the conscience requires intent to harm the violator without justification for deadly force.
What did Justice Souter's balancing test in Lewis weigh?
The cost of the pursuit against the value of the stolen property
The officer's level of training against the violator's record
The speed of the pursuit against how long it had already lasted
The need to stop a suspect against the danger to everyone in range

Lewis involved a minor offense and the death of a motorcycle passenger, and Justice Souter described the balancing test officers use to start, continue or end a pursuit: the need to stop a suspect against the high-speed danger to everyone in range.
In Scott v. Harris, what did Deputy Scott do?
Chased Harris for a traffic offense, then used a PIT at high speed
Pulled onto the main road from a side street to join the pursuit
Set up a roadblock around a curve with an 18-wheeler blocking it
Rammed Harris's motorcycle and killed the passenger riding on it
In Scott v. Harris (2007), Deputy Scott chased Victor Harris for a traffic offense at high speed for several minutes and then used a PIT at a much higher speed than PIT training recommends.
What did Justice Scalia say mattered in Scott v. Harris?
Whether Harris was in custody
Whether Scott followed agency policy
Whether Scott's actions were reasonable
Whether Scott's actions shocked the conscience

In Scott, Justice Scalia wrote that whether or not the act was deadly force, all that matters is whether it was reasonable, and rejected the argument that simply stopping the chase would have protected the public.
Why doesn't Scott v. Harris mean anything goes for Florida officers?
Scott v. Harris was later overturned by the Court's ruling in Lewis
The Scott decision applies only to sheriff's deputies, not officers
Florida law bans every pursuit that starts with a traffic offense
Florida officers are bound by Pinellas Park's negligence standard

Florida officers are bound by Pinellas Park's negligence standard, so Scott does not allow an 'anything goes' approach; under the Fourth Amendment, though, injury to a fleeing driver is generally not considered unreasonable force.
You start a pursuit. What must you do on the radio?
Stay off the radio entirely so you can focus on your driving
Contact only your supervisor and leave dispatch out of it
Report the pursuit on the radio only after it has ended
Tell dispatch, and stay in contact with dispatch and other units

In a pursuit, tell dispatch when you start or stop it, activate and properly use all emergency equipment, and stay in contact with dispatch and assisting units the whole time about changes or help needed.
How do you control speed and distance during a pursuit?
Pace the violator using the six-second rule
Stay just one car length behind the violator
Match the violator's speed exactly at all times
Keep a gap set by the three-second rule
Control your vehicle and speed by pacing the violator, using the six-second rule to keep a safe distance.
As a pursuit drags on, what risks grow?
Tire wear and low washer fluid
A low fuel level and overheating
Battery drain and radio failure
Brake fade and loss of traction
The longer a pursuit lasts, the greater the chance of brake fade or lost traction, and you must change your driving for nighttime conditions.
When must you end a pursuit?
As soon as the violator crosses out of your jurisdiction
As soon as a supervisor arrives on the scene to take over
Once the pursuit passes a set number of miles in length
As soon as the risk outweighs the benefit of the arrest
Stop the pursuit right away once the danger to the public, to you or to fellow officers is greater than the value of catching the violator.
How do some Florida agencies end pursuits more safely?
Always waiting for the violator to run out of fuel
Following at triple the six-second distance
Trained, policy-governed forcible-stop techniques
Asking the public to block the road
Some Florida agencies use tactics and technologies to end pursuits more safely and quickly, with training and policy governing forcible-stop techniques.
What is the purpose of a roadblock?
Slow down the traffic as it approaches a construction zone
Give the pursuing officers a safe place to stop and rest
Force the fleeing car to crash so that the pursuit ends at once
Show overwhelming strength so the violator stops and surrenders
A roadblock uses vehicles, barricades, cones or other objects to partly or completely block traffic, showing overwhelming law enforcement strength and position so the violator stops and surrenders.
Under Brower, what must a roadblock give the violator?
Enough time to stop
A choice of lanes
A warning on the radio
A way around the block
Under Brower, a roadblock must give the violator enough time to stop; roadblocks endanger officers, other drivers, pedestrians and the violator, so choose and set up the location carefully.
Which is an appropriate place for a roadblock?
In the middle of a sharp curve on a county road
Around a blind bend where trees block the view
A straight road with a clear view from both sides
Just over the crest of a hill on a two-lane road
A good roadblock site can be seen clearly from both directions on a highway, street or road; a bad site sits over a hilltop or in, on or near a curve.
Setting a roadblock, which action is forbidden?
Telling every pursuing officer the technique being used
Using marked law enforcement vehicles to form the block
Choosing a site with a clear view from both directions
Staying seated in a vehicle used to block the road

Never set a roadblock where the violator gets no warning unless deadly force is necessary, never block the road with equipment that is not law enforcement's, and never sit in a vehicle used as a block.
Why must the roadblock officers and pursuing officers communicate?
So the local media can be warned about the roadblock
So the violator hears the plan on a police scanner
Everyone needs to know which technique is being used
So dispatch can decide to end the pursuit for them
Communication between the roadblock officers and the pursuing officers is vital, and everyone in the pursuit should know the roadblock technique being used.
What sets the guidelines for using tire deflation devices?
Your agency's policy and training
The brand chosen by the manufacturer
The holding in Brower v. County of Inyo
The state law that covers roadblocks
Many brands of tire deflation devices exist, and agency policy and training set the guidelines for using them.
Where does a PIT make contact with the violator's car?
The center of the rear bumper
The driver's door
The front bumper
The right or left rear side
The pursuit immobilization technique (PIT) uses the patrol car to push the right or left rear of the fleeing car to stop the pursuit; use it only when trained and permitted by agency policy.
After a pursuit, what does the chapter say about reporting?
Reporting depends entirely on the outcome
Report the details promptly; it is always required
Report only if a PIT was used
Report only if property was damaged
Report pursuit details to your agency promptly; reporting policies differ, but prompt reporting is always required.
Which term means: An agency checklist officers complete each time they use an agency vehicle, used to remember what to check and to report failing equipment?
Public safety telecommunicator
PSI
Tire wear bars
Inspection form
Most agencies require officers to fill out an inspection form whenever they use an agency vehicle; it reminds them what to check and lets them report equipment that is failing.
Which term means: Pounds per square inch, the unit tire inflation is measured in; the recommended level is on the doorjamb?
PSI
Inspection form
Acuity
Tire wear bars
Tire inflation is measured in PSI (pounds per square inch); tires should be at or above the manufacturer's recommended PSI, which is listed on the doorjamb.
Which term means: Raised bars in the tread; once they sit flush with the tread surface, the tire can no longer move water away?
PSI
Tire wear bars
Inspection form
Depth perception
Once the wear bars sit flush with the tread, the tire can no longer channel water and other fluids away.
Which term means: How sharp a person's vision is?
Depth perception
Acuity
Peripheral vision
Color vision
Acuity is how sharp your vision is.
Which term means: Judging distance and space to tell how far away something is?
Acuity
Night vision
Color vision
Depth perception
Depth perception is judging distance and space to tell how far away an object is.
Which term means: Seeing above, below and to the sides; about 180 degrees for a driver with good side vision in a stopped car?
Depth perception
Acuity
Color vision
Peripheral vision
Peripheral vision lets you see up, down and off to each side; with good peripheral vision, a seated driver in a stopped car takes in about 180 degrees.
Which term means: The ability to tell colors apart?
Night vision
Acuity
Depth perception
Color vision
Color vision is telling colors apart, and night vision is seeing clearly in the dark.
Which term means: The ability to see clearly in the dark?
Night vision
Color vision
Acuity
Depth perception
Color vision is telling colors apart, and night vision is seeing clearly in the dark.
Which term means: Another name for the dispatcher you notify when you pull off the road for a vehicle safety hazard?
Color vision
Depth perception
Public safety telecommunicator
Acuity
If you find a safety hazard with the vehicle, pull off the road to a safe place and notify dispatch (the public safety telecommunicator), following agency policy.
Which term means: Tires riding on water instead of the road, so the car pulls to one side or does not hold at all?
Public safety telecommunicator
Three-second rule
Hydroplaning
Peripheral vision
Tires are built to disperse water but can still hydroplane, pulling to one side or not holding at all.
Which term means: The car ahead passes a fixed point and you count three seconds before reaching it?
Early apex
Apex
Three-second rule
Six-second rule
If you reach or pass the fixed point before you finish counting three seconds, pick a new point and count again; passing it after three seconds means a safe distance.
Which term means: The same counting method stretched to six seconds for poor conditions, higher speeds, emergency responses and similar situations?
Late apex
Six-second rule
Constant radius
Three-second rule
In poor road conditions or bad weather use the six-second rule; you count the same way, but count to six once the car ahead passes your fixed point.
Which term means: The roughly 6-inch-square area where each tire meets the road; every force on the vehicle acts through these four patches?
Center of gravity
Increasing radius
Tire contact patch
Decreasing radius
Most patrol vehicles ride on four tire contact patches of about 6 inches square each, and every force acting on the vehicle works through those four small areas.
Which term means: Front-to-rear or rear-to-front weight shift when accelerating or braking?
Pitch
Oversteer
